title: Shared religious practice and value alignment appear as relationship infrastructure, not only private belief
source_unit: Institute for Family Studies, Churchgoing husbands and wives are happier, September 25, 2026 insight

denominator.unit: married adults in the underlying study; public IFS insight does not state the sample size

marital_happiness_churchgoing_husbands.unit: percent of churchgoing husbands describing their marriage as very or extremely happy

marital_happiness_churchgoing_wives.unit: percent of churchgoing wives describing their marriage as very or extremely happy

marital_happiness_infrequent_or_nonatten.unit: percent of husbands attending church infrequently or never describing their marriage as very or extremely happy
percent of wives attending church infrequently or never describing their marriage as very or extremely happy

mechanism.value: Recurring communal practice may provide shared time, meaning and social reinforcement that couples can experience as relationship infrastructure

observations.method: IFS public insight summarizing a recent study and reporting subgroup percentages; the public listing does not provide the underlying study's sample size, full instrument, field dates or model specification.
observations.uncertainty: The reported differences are associational and may reflect selection, relationship stability, socioeconomic composition, prior beliefs or other unmeasured factors; the public insight does not establish that church attendance causes marital happiness.
observations.subgroup: Married U.S. adults ages 20–54, with potentially different patterns by denomination, race, class, education, age, sexuality, geography, attendance intensity and relationship history; subgroup estimates are not supplied in the public insight.
observations.counterinterpretation: Church attendance may be a marker for shared networks, values or selection into marriage rather than the operative cause; couples can also build shared meaning through nonreligious institutions and practices.

denominator.unit: married couples in the underlying study

shared_core_values.value: Spouses' agreement on core marriage and faith values is described as one of the strongest predictors of marital happiness

mechanism.value: Institutional practice appears most consequential when it creates a shared interpretive frame and coordinated expectations, rather than functioning as an isolated attendance behavior

institutional_translation.value: Family, faith and other communal institutions may shape wellbeing through repeated opportunities for alignment, obligation, recognition and social support

observations.method: Interpretive reading of the IFS insight's statement about value agreement and marital happiness; no underlying coefficients or causal design are available on the public page.
observations.uncertainty: The public source does not permit comparison of effect sizes, temporal ordering, mediation or whether shared values precede or follow relationship satisfaction.
observations.subgroup: Couples with different religious identities, attendance patterns, value conflicts and access to supportive communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Agreement may sometimes reflect conformity or suppressed conflict; disagreement can also be productive when couples have communication and institutional support.

denominator.unit: bounded interpretation of the reported relationship pattern

belonging_route.value: When communal practice supplies shared time and meaning, it can operate as a belonging route alongside family, neighborhood, civic, cultural and voluntary organizations

consumer_effect.value: Institutions that provide trustworthy recurring spaces may influence household time allocation, service choice and willingness to contribute, but the source does not measure consumer behavior

political_effect.value: Communal institutions can create relational capacity for care and civic voice, but the source does not measure political participation, policy preferences or institutional power

observations.method: Program interpretation, explicitly separated from the IFS-reported percentages and association claims.
observations.uncertainty: No evidence here identifies downstream effects on fertility, household spending, social trust, civic participation, service use or public policy.
observations.subgroup: Households and communities with different religious and nonreligious forms of recurring social infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strong communal institutions can support belonging but can also impose exclusionary norms or unequal burdens; this source does not measure either outcome.

related_sources.claim: Public IFS insight with the reported happiness percentages, age range and statement about spouses' agreement on core marriage and faith values.

boundary: This record identifies a communal-practice, shared-values and relationship-infrastructure subtheme. It does not establish causality, sample representativeness, effect sizes, temporal ordering, fertility or household-consumption effects, civic participation, institutional inclusion or superiority of religious over nonreligious forms of social connection.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official IFS insight page was reviewed for the September 25, 2026 date, title, reported percentages for churchgoing and infrequently or never attending husbands and wives, age range and value-agreement statement.
